subject: Web Development
courseTitle: Famous Websites That Changed the World

hook.text: On December 20, 1990, the world's first website went live at info.cern.ch.

buildup.text: It was plain text with blue hyperlinks explaining what the World Wide Web was.

discovery.text: No images, no design, no style. Just text describing how to use this new invention.

twist.text: The original page was lost for years. CERN launched a project in 2013 to restore it.

climax.text: That humble text page became the seed of an industry worth trillions of dollars.

punchline.text: The web's first page explained the web itself.

quiz.question: What was the first website about?

hook.text: In 1994, two Stanford students started organizing websites into categories by hand.

buildup.text: Jerry Yang and David Filo built Yahoo as a human-curated directory of the growing web.

discovery.text: Yahoo became the starting page for millions. If your site was listed, traffic poured in.

twist.text: Yahoo turned down a chance to buy Google for $1 million in 1998. It was 'too small.'

climax.text: Human curation couldn't scale. Algorithms replaced librarians, and Yahoo faded into history.

punchline.text: The web's first guide couldn't keep up with it.

hook.text: GeoCities gave anyone a free web page, organized into virtual neighborhoods.

buildup.text: Hollywood for entertainment, SiliconValley for tech — pick a theme and start building.

discovery.text: Millions built pages with animated GIFs, guest books, and 'Under Construction' signs.

twist.text: Yahoo bought GeoCities for $3.6 billion, then shut it down in 2009.

climax.text: Archivists saved fragments, but most of the early personal web vanished overnight.

punchline.text: Millions of personal pages vanished in one decision.

hook.text: Craig Newmark started an email list about San Francisco events in 1995.

buildup.text: It grew into a website for housing, jobs, and selling anything — plain text, no frills.

discovery.text: Craigslist destroyed newspaper classified sections by offering the same service for free.

twist.text: The site's design hasn't changed in 25 years. It still looks like it was built in 1999.

climax.text: Craigslist proved that function beats aesthetics. Usefulness matters more than beauty.

punchline.text: An ugly site killed an entire newspaper industry.

hook.text: Pierre Omidyar's first eBay sale was a broken laser pointer for $14.83 in 1995.

buildup.text: eBay created an auction marketplace where anyone could sell anything to anyone worldwide.

discovery.text: The reputation system — buyer and seller ratings — made strangers trust each other online.

twist.text: The buyer of that broken laser pointer knew it was broken. He collected broken laser pointers.

climax.text: eBay proved that trust systems could power an entirely new kind of global economy.

punchline.text: An online reputation system built a global market.

hook.text: In 1998, two Stanford PhD students ranked web pages by counting who linked to them.

buildup.text: PageRank treated links as votes. More links from important pages meant higher rankings.

discovery.text: Google's results were dramatically better than Yahoo, AltaVista, or any other search engine.

twist.text: Google's home page was almost empty — just a logo and a search box. That simplicity was radical.

climax.text: Google became a verb. 'Just Google it' replaced 'look it up' in everyday language.

punchline.text: A college project became the world's front door.

hook.text: Jimmy Wales launched Wikipedia in 2001 with a radical idea: anyone can edit any article.

buildup.text: Volunteers wrote millions of articles in hundreds of languages, all for free.

discovery.text: Wikipedia became the sixth most visited website and the largest encyclopedia in history.

twist.text: Experts predicted chaos. Instead, the community developed governance to maintain quality.

climax.text: Wikipedia proved that collective knowledge, freely shared, could rival professional encyclopedias.

punchline.text: Volunteers built the world's largest encyclopedia.

hook.text: Joel Spolsky and Jeff Atwood noticed developers wasted hours searching for coding answers.

buildup.text: Stack Overflow launched in 2008 as a Q&A site where the best answers rise to the top.

discovery.text: Gamification — reputation points and badges — motivated experts to answer for free.

twist.text: A study found that a typical developer visits Stack Overflow multiple times per day.

climax.text: Stack Overflow became the world's largest developer knowledge base, shaping how code gets written.

punchline.text: Developers taught each other and built the web.

quiz.question: What motivates experts to answer on Stack Overflow?

hook.text: The web forgets. Pages disappear, links break, and digital history vanishes.

buildup.text: Brewster Kahle founded the Internet Archive in 1996 to preserve the web's history.

discovery.text: The Wayback Machine has saved over 800 billion web pages spanning nearly three decades.

twist.text: The Internet Archive also lends digital books, sparking lawsuits from publishers.

climax.text: Without Archive.org, most of the early web's history would be permanently erased.

punchline.text: One nonprofit saved the web's memory for everyone.

quiz.question: What does the Wayback Machine preserve?
options: Snapshots of web pages over time

hook.text: Before GitHub, sharing code meant emailing zip files or managing complex server setups.

buildup.text: GitHub made Git — a version control tool — social, visual, and easy for teams.

discovery.text: Open source exploded. Anyone could fork a project, make changes, and submit a pull request.

twist.text: Microsoft bought GitHub for $7.5 billion in 2018. The open source world held its breath.

climax.text: GitHub became the world's largest code repository, hosting over 200 million projects.

punchline.text: Code sharing built the modern web's foundation.

hook.text: MySpace launched in 2003 and let users customize profiles with their own HTML and CSS.

buildup.text: Bands uploaded music, teens built digital identities, and the site hit 100 million users.

discovery.text: MySpace taught a generation that the web was personal — your profile was your digital home.

twist.text: News Corp bought MySpace for $580 million. Poor management drove users straight to Facebook.

climax.text: MySpace proved social networks could be massive — and that corporate owners could destroy them.

punchline.text: The first social giant fell to bad management.

quiz.question: What made MySpace unique?
options: Users could customize profiles with HTML

hook.text: In 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched Facebook from a Harvard dorm room. It required a .edu email.

buildup.text: Unlike MySpace, Facebook used real names and real identities. Authenticity was the feature.

discovery.text: The News Feed, launched in 2006, turned the web into a real-time stream of friends' updates.

twist.text: Facebook's data practices led to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, shaking public trust.

climax.text: With three billion users, Facebook reshaped how humanity communicates and consumes information.

punchline.text: Real names built real power — and real problems.

quiz.question: What feature made Facebook different from MySpace?

hook.text: Jack Dorsey sent the first tweet on March 21, 2006: 'just setting up my twttr.'

buildup.text: The 140-character limit forced brevity. Ideas had to be sharp to fit.

discovery.text: Twitter became the place where news broke first — often before television or newspapers.

twist.text: The same openness that powered revolutions also enabled misinformation at massive scale.

climax.text: Twitter proved that real-time public conversation could reshape politics and culture.

punchline.text: A character limit shaped global conversation.

quiz.question: What was Twitter's original character limit?

topics.title: Reddit: The Front Page of the Internet

hook.text: Reddit launched in 2005 as a link-sharing site with user voting to surface the best content.

buildup.text: Subreddits let communities form around any topic — from science to memes to knitting.

discovery.text: Upvotes and downvotes created a democratic ranking system driven entirely by users.

twist.text: Reddit's anonymity enabled both deep honesty and toxic behavior in equal measure.

climax.text: Reddit proved that niche communities could thrive at massive scale on a single platform.

punchline.text: Democracy and anonymity created a chaotic forum.

hook.text: Reid Hoffman launched LinkedIn in 2003 to bring professional networking online.

buildup.text: Users created digital resumes, connected with colleagues, and searched for jobs.

discovery.text: Recruiters adopted it rapidly. LinkedIn became the default way to find and vet job candidates.

twist.text: Microsoft bought LinkedIn for $26.2 billion — the largest tech acquisition at the time.

climax.text: LinkedIn turned the resume from a paper document into a living, searchable profile.

punchline.text: A website replaced the paper resume forever.

hook.text: Jeff Bezos started Amazon in his garage in 1994, selling only books.

buildup.text: One-click ordering and customer reviews made online shopping feel safe and convenient.

discovery.text: Amazon expanded into everything — electronics, groceries, streaming, and cloud computing.

twist.text: Amazon Web Services, built to run the store, became its most profitable business.

climax.text: Amazon redefined retail, logistics, and cloud computing from a single website.

punchline.text: A bookstore became the world's everything store.

hook.text: In 1999, sending money online meant mailing a check or wiring through a bank.

buildup.text: PayPal let users send money with just an email address. No bank visits required.

discovery.text: eBay sellers adopted PayPal so fast that eBay eventually bought the company for $1.5 billion.

twist.text: PayPal's founding team — Musk, Thiel, Levchin — went on to shape Silicon Valley for decades.

climax.text: PayPal proved that people would trust a website with their money if the experience was easy.

punchline.text: An email address became a bank account.

hook.text: Tobias Lutke wanted to sell snowboards online but found existing tools painful to use.

buildup.text: He built his own platform, then realized other merchants needed the same thing.

discovery.text: Shopify let anyone launch an online store without knowing how to code.

twist.text: During COVID, Shopify's revenue doubled as physical stores rushed online to survive.

climax.text: Shopify democratized e-commerce, powering millions of stores from garage brands to global names.

punchline.text: A snowboard shop built the world's store builder.

quiz.question: What was Shopify's founder originally selling?

hook.text: Processing credit cards on the web used to require a merchant account and weeks of paperwork.

buildup.text: Patrick and John Collison built Stripe so developers could accept payments in seven lines of code.

discovery.text: Stripe handled fraud detection, compliance, and global currencies behind a simple API.

twist.text: Two brothers from rural Ireland built a $95 billion company that powers internet commerce.

climax.text: Stripe made online payments invisible. Millions of businesses run on it without users knowing.

punchline.text: Seven lines of code unlocked global commerce.

hook.text: Brian Chesky couldn't afford rent. He put air mattresses in his living room for conference guests.

buildup.text: Airbnb let anyone rent out a spare room or entire home to travelers worldwide.

discovery.text: Reviews, photos, and identity verification made people trust sleeping in a stranger's home.

twist.text: Cities fought back with regulations. Airbnb disrupted not just hotels, but housing markets.

climax.text: Airbnb proved that trust and design could turn any home into a hotel room.

punchline.text: Air mattresses launched a hospitality empire.

quiz.question: How did Airbnb start?
options: Renting air mattresses during a conference

hook.text: Three former PayPal employees wanted an easy way to share video clips online.

buildup.text: YouTube launched in 2005 with a simple upload button and a Flash-based video player.

discovery.text: The first viral hit — 'Lazy Sunday' from SNL — proved video could spread like wildfire online.

twist.text: Google bought YouTube for $1.65 billion in 2006. Many called it overpaying. It was a bargain.

climax.text: YouTube replaced television for an entire generation and created the creator economy.

punchline.text: Upload a video and the world can watch it.

quiz.question: How much did Google pay for YouTube?

topics.title: Netflix: From DVDs to Streaming Giant

hook.text: Netflix started in 1997 mailing DVDs in red envelopes. No late fees, no store visits.

buildup.text: In 2007, Netflix launched streaming. Watch instantly — no disc, no waiting.

discovery.text: Recommendation algorithms learned your taste and kept you watching for hours.

twist.text: Blockbuster turned down a chance to buy Netflix for $50 million. Blockbuster went bankrupt.

climax.text: Netflix killed the video rental industry and redefined how the world consumes entertainment.

punchline.text: DVDs in envelopes killed the video store.

quiz.question: What did Blockbuster do when offered Netflix?

hook.text: Napster showed people wanted digital music. Spotify showed them they didn't need to own it.

buildup.text: For a monthly fee, listeners got access to millions of songs instantly, legally.

discovery.text: Playlists replaced albums. Algorithmic discovery introduced listeners to artists they'd never find.

twist.text: Artists complained that Spotify pays fractions of a penny per stream. The economics are brutal.

climax.text: Spotify transformed music from a product you buy into a service you rent.

punchline.text: Streaming replaced ownership for a generation.

quiz.question: What did Spotify change about music consumption?

hook.text: Justin Kan strapped a camera to his head in 2007 and streamed his entire life online.

buildup.text: Justin.tv pivoted to gaming streams. Twitch was born — a site for watching people play.

discovery.text: Chat interaction made viewers feel like part of the action, not passive observers.

twist.text: Amazon bought Twitch for $970 million, outbidding Google. Live gaming was serious business.

climax.text: Twitch proved that watching someone play a game could be as entertaining as playing it.

punchline.text: Watching became the new playing.

hook.text: Matt Mullenweg was 19 when he forked a blogging tool and created WordPress in 2003.

buildup.text: Themes and plugins let non-developers build professional websites without writing code.

discovery.text: WordPress powers over 40% of all websites on the internet — from blogs to Fortune 500 sites.

twist.text: WordPress is open source. No company owns it. A nonprofit foundation stewards the project.

climax.text: WordPress democratized publishing more than any technology since the printing press.

punchline.text: A teenager's project runs 40% of the web.

quiz.question: What percentage of websites does WordPress power?

topics.title: Uber: A Ride at a Tap

hook.text: Travis Kalanick couldn't find a cab in Paris. He decided to fix the problem with an app.

buildup.text: Uber let anyone request a ride from their phone. A driver appeared in minutes.

discovery.text: GPS, mobile payments, and ratings made the experience seamless and trustworthy.

twist.text: Taxi industries worldwide protested and sued. Uber operated in legal gray zones for years.

climax.text: Uber proved that a web-connected app could replace a century-old transportation system.

punchline.text: An app replaced a century of taxi dispatching.

quiz.question: What traditional industry did Uber disrupt?

hook.text: Design tools were desktop applications that couldn't share work in real time.

buildup.text: Figma put the entire design tool in a browser tab. Anyone with a link could view and edit.

discovery.text: Real-time collaboration meant designers and developers worked on the same file simultaneously.

twist.text: Adobe tried to buy Figma for $20 billion but regulators blocked the deal.

climax.text: Figma proved that even professional creative tools could move entirely to the web.

punchline.text: A browser tab replaced a desktop application.

quiz.question: What makes Figma different from traditional design tools?
options: It runs entirely in the browser
It uses AI to design automatically

hook.text: Teams juggled separate apps for docs, wikis, tasks, and databases. Notion combined them.

buildup.text: Everything is a block — text, tables, Kanban boards, and embeds — all on one flexible page.

discovery.text: Templates let teams spin up project trackers, meeting notes, and wikis in seconds.

twist.text: Notion nearly died in 2016 when it ran out of funding. The founders rebuilt it from scratch in Japan.

climax.text: Notion showed that a single web app could replace an entire suite of productivity tools.

punchline.text: One app replaced a dozen tools for millions.

topics.title: ChatGPT: AI Comes to the Web

hook.text: On November 30, 2022, OpenAI launched a chatbot. It reached 100 million users in two months.

buildup.text: ChatGPT could write essays, explain code, and hold conversations that felt almost human.

discovery.text: It was delivered as a simple web app — just a text box and a submit button.

twist.text: The simplest possible web interface for the most complex AI model. Design echoed Google's homepage.

climax.text: ChatGPT proved that the web browser remains the best way to deliver transformative technology.

punchline.text: A text box delivered an AI revolution.

quiz.question: How quickly did ChatGPT reach 100 million users?

topics.title: The Website That Hasn't Been Built Yet

hook.text: Every world-changing website started as someone's side project or wild idea.

buildup.text: Google was a research project. Facebook was a dorm experiment. Shopify was a snowboard store.

discovery.text: The web's low barrier to entry means the next big idea could come from anywhere.

twist.text: You don't need permission, a factory, or investors to put something on the web.

climax.text: The most important website ever built might be the one someone is starting today.

punchline.text: The next world-changing site hasn't launched yet.

quiz.question: What do all world-changing websites have in common?
